00 — CORRECTION

A data issue, found and fixed

The first pass of this analysis had a bug: three ledger entries booked against an internal cash code (not a real security) were mis-read as trades in a phantom holding, which briefly showed up internally as roughly –154,000 "shares" of something called "Cash." That's likely what looked wrong. The root cause was a matured cash instrument (a short-term note, code 513507) that got redeemed and partially reversed in your December 2025 ledger — the redemption and its correction were tagged with a cash-account label instead of a security name.

What changed: that cash code is now fully excluded from sector and holdings calculations. A second, smaller issue was also fixed: ₪177,327 of securities transferred into the account in early 2023 (before the balance file's tracking window begins) were being dropped from the running cost-basis totals — they're now correctly included. Sector allocation, holdings, and realized P&L numbers below are all restated. A genuine cash reconciliation is added in Section 08 so the actual cash position is visible and checkable, rather than implied.
01 — OVERVIEW

Three years, roughly tripled — and ahead of the market

The account grew from ₪325,261 to ₪1,091,209 over three years. Stripping out the ₪373,000 you deposited, the portfolio's true performance — its time-weighted return — was +74.3% in shekels, or +116.4% measured in the dollars the portfolio actually trades in. That beats a passive S&P 500 hold (69%) and even the red-hot Nasdaq-100 (100%) over the identical window — see Section 06.

Because contributions were steady and reasonably well-timed (32 deposits averaging ~₪11.7K), the money-weighted return (XIRR) of +21.5% sits slightly above the annualized time-weighted figure. The ride was not smooth: annualized volatility ran 19% and the portfolio sat through a -24.7% peak-to-trough drawdown, consistent with the heavy technology and semiconductor tilt in Section 04.

02 — VALUE OVER TIME

Daily, monthly and yearly value

Viewed at daily resolution, the equity curve shows the steady 2024 grind higher, the sharp April-2025 tariff shock and rebound, a summer-2025 surge to fresh highs, and a strong spring-2026 leg that carried the account past ₪1.0M. A key wrinkle is currency: most holdings are USD-denominated, yet the account is reported in shekels, and the shekel strengthened from 3.70 to 2.98 per dollar over the period — a headwind on the shekel-reported value, which is why the portfolio's dollar return outpaces its shekel return.

03 — RETURNS & RISK

What the performance actually looked like

The "growth of 100" curve is the cleanest read on skill versus deposits: 100 invested at the start became 174 in shekel terms. Annual time-weighted returns were positive every full year — +23.9% in 2024 and +20.3% in 2025 (NIS) — with 2023 and 2026 being partial years. The monthly heatmap exposes the real volatility underneath those clean annual numbers: a brutal Feb–Mar 2025, the near-flat April 2025 where a +13.7% single-day rebound almost exactly offset the early-month tariff crash, and a powerful +15.8% April 2026.

04 — SECTOR ANALYSIS (corrected)

Diversification and where the gains came from

The portfolio is fundamentally a technology and semiconductor book, built on top of a diversified ETF/index-fund core that was transferred in at account opening. The multi-line diversification chart shows active rotation: the semiconductor allocation was built up through 2024–25 to a peak near ₪210K of cost basis, then trimmed in early 2026, while Technology, Communication Services and a new Financials position were scaled up. The original ETF sleeve was steadily sold down as capital rotated into individual names — it remains the single largest bucket at ₪185K mostly because it was the largest starting position, not because it grew.

On the return side, semiconductors were the standout, with ₪181,381 in realized gains — a large block crystallized in the early-2026 rotation — followed by the original ETF sleeve at ₪104,995. Technology shows a small realized loss at the close: some positions were trimmed or rebought at a loss even as the broad tech tape rose. These lines capture realized gains plus dividends only — unrealized gains on still-held positions aren't included, since the source data has no daily per-security prices.

06 — VS. THE MARKET

How does this compare to just buying an index fund?

Over the identical window, the S&P 500 returned 69% and the Nasdaq-100 (with dividends) returned 100%, both in USD, both price/total-return only (no new money added). Your portfolio's own USD time-weighted return of +116% beat both.

That's a clean, deposit-free comparison. The more concrete question is: what if the exact same deposits, on the exact same dates, had simply been put into an index fund instead? The simulation below answers that — it takes your real contribution schedule and buys the benchmark on each contribution date.

+₪228,844 ahead of the S&P 500

On identical deposits and dates, your actual portfolio is worth ₪1,091,209 today ($366,177) versus ₪862,365 ($289,384) had the same money simply bought the S&P 500, and ₪999,874 ($335,528) had it bought the Nasdaq-100.

The year-by-year view adds nuance the headline number hides: 2023–24 was essentially market-matching (a "closet indexer" period), and 2025 is where the outperformance was actually made — a +37.6% year against a +16.4% S&P 500 and +21.0% Nasdaq-100, almost entirely the semiconductor rotation documented in Section 04. 2026 has continued that edge so far.

For local context: the Tel Aviv 125 — which this portfolio also holds directly via index funds — had an extraordinary run of its own, +51% in 2025 alone (Ctech/Calcalist, citing Nasdaq Index Research data) on top of +~30% in 2024, so home-market returns were exceptional too, though on a different currency basis than the USD comparisons above.

Methodology. S&P 500 uses FRED's daily close series (price return, dividends not included — a small, ~1.3%/yr understatement vs. a real S&P 500 fund). Nasdaq-100 uses Nasdaq's own published monthly total-return figures (dividends included), linearly interpolated to daily for the chart; April–June 2026 is one combined quarterly figure backed out from YTD data pending a monthly breakdown. The cash-flow-matched simulation converts each NIS deposit to USD at that day's rate and "buys" the benchmark at that day's level, then compounds forward — the same money, the same 32 dates, a different destination.

08 — COSTS, CASH & TRADING ACTIVITY

What the trading cost — and where the cash sits

Costs were strikingly low. Total commissions over three years and 226 executed trades came to just ₪1,261 — on roughly ₪1,716K of buys and ₪1,455K of sells, an all-in commission rate of about 4.0 basis points of turnover. The larger cost line was margin / debit interest of ₪8,423, incurred on periods of negative cash balance — visible as the red dip below zero in the cash-reconciliation chart in Section 00, which bottomed at ₪-57,402 around 2024-09-04.

Methodology & caveats. Built from two source files: a daily NIS balance series (900 trading days) and 715 ledger transactions. Time-weighted return (TWR) chains daily returns with external deposits removed on their settlement day. XIRR is the money-weighted internal rate of return on the actual deposit cash-flow schedule plus start/end values. The USD series divides the NIS value by a daily USD/ILS rate interpolated from FX rates stamped on USD transactions. Sector cost basis and realized P&L use average-cost lot matching, now correctly including securities transferred in before the balance file's tracking window (Jan–Jun 2023) and correctly excluding two internal cash-ledger bookkeeping codes that are not real securities. Realized-return charts exclude unrealized gains on still-held positions. Benchmark data: S&P 500 from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), Nasdaq-100 total return from Nasdaq's official index fact sheet, TA-125 annual figures from Ctech/Calcalist. Volatility and Sharpe/Sortino assume 252 trading days and a 0% risk-free rate.

This document is a descriptive analysis of historical account data for your own information. It is not investment advice, a recommendation, or a solicitation, and past performance does not predict future results.
